opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the scope is actually one of the most important design questions, and people often get it wrong by thinking too narrowly. The instinct is to write policies at the level of individual tool calls: can the agent call this API, can it run this SQL query, can it send this email. That's necessary, but it's not sufficient, because the risk usually isn't in any single action. It's in the combination of what the agent can read, what it can write, and who it can talk to.

So I like to think about it in a few layers. First, there's the data the agent can see. If an agent can read sensitive customer records and can also send messages to the outside world, you've basically created an exfiltration path, even if each permission looks fine on its own. So policies have to reason about information flow, not just access.

Second, there's whose authority the agent is acting under. In a lot of enterprise settings, the right default is that the agent should never have more permissions than the user who invoked it, and often less. It should inherit the user's identity and governance rules rather than running as some all-powerful service account. That's very much how we think about it in data platforms: the same access controls, lineage, and auditing you apply to humans and jobs should apply to agents.

Third, there's the scope of the task. An agent working on "summarize last quarter's sales" doesn't need write access to anything. So you want policies that can be scoped dynamically to the task, kind of like least privilege, but computed per request instead of set once by an admin.

And finally, you need observability and the ability to review. You won't get the policies perfect up front, so you need logging of every action, the ability to evaluate traces, and human-in-the-loop checkpoints for the high-stakes, irreversible stuff like moving money, deleting data, or contacting customers.

The broader point is that agents make governance more important, not less. A lot of what makes them safe to deploy is boring infrastructure: identity, permissions, lineage, and audit, applied consistently. The companies that already have that foundation in place are going to be able to give agents a lot more autonomy, a lot faster.

r001.rationale: The response discusses permissions and logging agent actions, but does not state that policies can intercept any event generated by the agent.

r002.rationale: The response mentions logging, traces, lineage, and auditing, but does not state that policies can maintain tracking state.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that "policy" is a pretty overloaded word here, and when people talk about controlling an agent they're often actually talking about three or four different layers at once.

The way I think about it, there's the narrowest layer, which is just what tools and what data the agent is allowed to touch at all. That's basically access control, and honestly it's the thing we understand best, because it's the same problem we've had with users and service accounts for decades. If the agent can't see a table or can't call a function, then no amount of clever prompting is going to get it there. So I always tell people to start there, because it's deterministic, it's auditable, and it doesn't depend on the model behaving.

Then there's a middle layer, which is what I'd call constraints on the sequence of actions. The agent can read this and it can write that, but it shouldn't do them in this combination, or it shouldn't take more than N steps, or it shouldn't spend more than some budget. That's where it gets more interesting, because now the policy has state. You're reasoning about a trajectory, not a single call, and that's something traditional permission systems really weren't built for.

And then there's the outermost layer, which is the fuzzy stuff. Don't be rude to the customer, don't make commitments the company can't keep. Those are things you can't really express as a rule over tool calls. You end up enforcing them either with the model itself, through instructions, or with a second model watching the first one. And I think the mistake a lot of people make is they try to push everything into that outer layer, because it's the most flexible, and then they're surprised when it's unreliable.

So the scoping question for me is really: how much of what you care about can you push down into the hard, deterministic layers, and how small can you make the part that depends on judgment? The more you can shrink that last part, the more confidence you can actually have. And it's also just a lot easier to test. You can write unit tests for "this agent never has write access to production." It's much harder to write a test for "this agent is always appropriately cautious."

The other thing I'd add is that scope should be task-specific, not agent-specific. An agent that's doing research for you and an agent that's executing a refund are very different risk profiles, even if it's the same underlying model. So I'd much rather see narrow policies attached to a workflow than one giant policy attached to "the assistant." It's more work up front, but it maps a lot better to how people actually reason about what could go wrong.

r001.rationale: The response discusses access control and constraints on action sequences, but does not state that policies can intercept any event generated by an agent.

r002.rationale: It says sequence-based policies have state and reason about an action trajectory rather than a single call, communicating that they can maintain tracking state.

astra-6.text:
I think you want policies at a few different levels. Some are about individual actions: can this agent read this data, can it send an email, can it modify something? But others are about the task as a whole. You might be allowed to read a document and allowed to send email, but that doesn’t mean you should be allowed to email that document to anyone.

So the scope has to include the context: who the agent is acting for, what they asked it to do, and where information is going. And ideally, you enforce those constraints outside the model, at the point where it accesses data or takes an action. The model can reason about what it should do, but you don’t want the entire security boundary to depend on it following an instruction.

r002.rationale: The response describes task context and enforcement, but does not state that policies can maintain tracking state.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the scope has to be broader than just what the model is allowed to say. Once an agent can take actions, you care about what data it can access, what tools it can call, and where it can send information. And those decisions often depend on the context: who the user is, what task they authorized, and what information the agent has encountered along the way.

For example, an agent might be allowed to read an internal document and also send email, but that doesn’t mean it should be allowed to email that document to anyone. The individual permissions aren’t enough; you need a policy about how they compose.

So I’d separate the model’s judgment from enforcement. The model can propose an action, but there should be a layer outside it that checks whether that action is permitted, and asks for approval when necessary. You want the agent to be flexible in how it solves a problem while keeping its authority bounded.

r001.rationale: The response describes an external layer checking proposed actions, but does not state that policies can intercept any event generated by the agent.

r002.rationale: It mentions context such as the user, task, and information encountered, but does not say that policies maintain tracking state.
